facts.text: The hero's name is a pun: Treat Williams plays Detective Roger Mortis, which sounds like "rigor mortis" and is also Latin for "death." Dead cop, dead-on name.
The film's theme song was written by John Huckert, Patrick Read Johnson and Phil Settle, and performed by Settle. Johnson also worked on the movie as visual effects supervisor.
Watch the store windows and the van in this first car scene: the film crew is briefly visible in the reflections.
Roger Mortis' undercover car is a 1960 Chevrolet Impala convertible. Even dead cops like a classic ride.
Director Mark Goldblatt was a veteran editor (The Terminator, RoboCop, The Howling) who got his start under Roger Corman at New World. Dead Heat was his directing debut.
Dead Heat was shot in just 37 days on a budget of about $5 million, effects-heavy zombie gore included.
The commentary track recalls a bumpy first day of shooting for Mel Stewart, who plays the cops' Captain Mayberry in this scene.
Dead Heat was reportedly put into production after the success of 1987's buddy-cop hit Lethal Weapon and the cop-and-alien thriller The Hidden.
Screenwriter Terry Black's little brother is Shane Black, the Lethal Weapon writer, who has a cameo here as a patrolman.
Darren McGavin (Dr. Ernest McNab) was TV's Kolchak: The Night Stalker, a reporter chasing monsters. Fitting that he runs a morgue full of walking dead here.
The building used for Dante Pharmaceuticals later appeared in the Pauly Shore comedy Bio-Dome, eight years after this film.
Lindsay Frost (Randi James) is the sister of Mark Frost, co-creator of Twin Peaks, and the daughter of actor Warren Frost.
Joe Piscopo was in his bodybuilding phase. Makeup effects artist Steve Johnson reportedly said Piscopo had a gym on wheels parked on set.
British stand-up comic Bernard Manning reportedly auditioned for Doug Bigelow, the role that went to Joe Piscopo.
Star Treat Williams was a real pilot: he flew professionally for a year in the early 1980s and became a certified flight instructor for planes and helicopters.
The filmmakers say they aimed more for horror than comedy and felt thwarted. A producer recalls another studio saw it as a flat-out comedy.
A promo reel for Dead Heat was scored with "Shakedown" from Beverly Hills Cop, hinting that studio New World was selling it as a comedy.
Visual effects artist Ernest Farino used his rotoscoping experience to create the lightning effects for the resurrection machine.
Roger is declared pulseless and doesn't bleed when cut here. Later he bleeds plenty when shot. Zombie physiology is inconsistent.
Director Mark Goldblatt's film suffered numerous gore cuts to win an R rating instead of an X.
Dead Heat cost about $5 million and earned roughly $3.59 million, a box office flop that later built a cult following on home video.
Co-star Joe Piscopo was a Saturday Night Live cast member from 1980 to 1984 and starred in the gangster spoof Johnny Dangerously.
When production fell behind schedule, Patrick Read Johnson took over as second unit director and directed this cleaver-wielding butcher scene.
Dead Heat's zombie-cop idea got name-checked later in the cult comedy Zombie Cop (1991) and Leslie Nielsen-less spoof Loaded Weapon 1 (1993).
A reviewer praised Treat Williams for playing monster-movie material with a wry tone, the same approach he later took in the creature feature Deep Rising (1998).
Composer Ernest Troost, who also scored Tremors, wrote the music. Director Mark Goldblatt reportedly forbade trumpets in the score.
TV versions extend this mausoleum sequence and add an appearance by B-movie regular Dick Miller, who is not in the theatrical cut.
Finding Doug dead and Randi explaining everything echoes the big reveal of the 1949 noir D.O.A., another story about a man who's been fatally poisoned and is hunting his killer.
The code number from the crypt, 2639362867, decodes on a phone keypad to "BODYDOC" (and the extra digits fit "BodyDoctor"), Dr. McNab's license plate.
New World asked screenwriter Terry Black for a sequel. He noted everyone dies at the end. The exec replied: "You've got a resurrection machine... you figure it out." It was never made.
Director Mark Goldblatt recalls a disappointing initial reception for Dead Heat, followed by a resurgence as a cult film.
After Dead Heat, director Mark Goldblatt directed The Punisher (1989), then returned to editing and earned an Oscar nomination for Terminator 2: Judgment Day.
Horror icon Vincent Price filmed all of his scenes as Arthur P. Loudermilk in just three days.
Makeup effects artist Steve Johnson made a life cast of Vincent Price for the film's effects.
Vincent Price also played Egghead on TV's Batman and the villain Professor Ratigan in Disney's The Great Mouse Detective (1986), two years before this film.
Darren McGavin (Dr. McNab) is famously uncredited in The Natural (1984) after a billing and salary dispute, yet billed here as a lead villain.
Roger's closing line, "Perhaps this is the end of a beautiful friendship," is the film's parody of Casablanca's famous final line.
Drive-In Totals verdict: Two and a half stars. Joe Bob says check it out.
